## Role of this chapter

- Institutional background (Colombian corporate tax system, 1980s) and data description that every later chapter leans on, so it isn't repeated in ch. 4-8.
- Two things downstream chapters cite directly: the juridical-organization split (corps = truth-reporters, used from @sec-testing onward) and the ST-liable/exempt industry split (used in @sec-fiscal).

Colombian manufacturing in 1981–1991 offers a unique setting to study tax evasion by overreporting deductible inputs. First, a sales tax that worked as a value-added tax and rewarded overreporting materials: manufacturers could reduce the tax they owed on their sales by claiming fictitious deductions (@sec-setting-incentive). Second, a truth-reporting group of firms: corporations, which government and market scrutiny kept from evading (@sec-setting-jo). Third, variation in the tax rate: the 1983 reform raised the sales-tax rate for most industries but left food products exempt (@sec-setting-st). Finally, firm-level records of output and inputs, together with legal form and taxes paid (@sec-setting-data). Because the approach uses the production function, it applies to any data with firms' output and inputs, such as surveys, administrative data, or tax records.

## Data {#sec-setting-data}

I use the Colombian Annual Survey of Manufacturing (EAM), a panel of manufacturing plants with more than 10 employees from 1981 to 1991.^[The survey's unit of observation is the plant; I refer to plants and firms interchangeably.] The EAM records, for each plant, the output and inputs that a production function needs, the plant's juridical organization, and the sales tax it charged on its sales and paid on its purchases.^[The year in the panel is the activity (reference) year. DANE runs the EAM each year with the economic year immediately preceding collection as the reference period [@DANE1995, p. 40]: the survey for year $x$ is collected during $x+1$ and labelled $x$ (e.g. the 1992–1994 surveys were collected in 1993–1995, and the 1992 file values assets at December 1992; @DANE2018).] The panel is well known: it has been used in seminal work on export dynamics, reallocation, and productivity, and to estimate production functions [@RobertsTybout1997; @Das2007; @Eslava2004; @Gandhi2020]. Similar to these studies, I observe inputs as firms reported them; in contrast, I ask how the tax incentives of the period, including the 1983 reform, shaped those reports. The working sample has 40,508 firm-years from 5,915 plants in 28 industries, covering the four juridical organizations described in @sec-setting-jo (@tbl-sum-stats).

![Summary statistics, manufacturing firms in Colombia (1981--1991).](/tables/ch03-summary-stats.png){#tbl-sum-stats}

## The sales tax: a credit on purchases {#sec-setting-incentive}

The Colombian sales tax worked as a value-added tax (VAT): manufacturers credited the tax paid on their purchases against the tax charged on their sales. The tax originally targeted the manufacturing sector, on finished goods and imports. From 1966, manufacturers could claim credit on the taxes paid on inputs *incorporated* into the product, and from 1974 on any purchase made by the firm, except the acquisition of capital goods; the credits worked through a system of refunds [@Perry1990, p. 180].

The credit rewards overreporting materials. An artificial increase in the reported value of materials raises the credit by $\tau_P$, the rate paid on purchases, pesos per peso, and reduces the firm's tax liability by as much. Since capital goods could not be credited and labour was not a taxed purchase, I assume firms overreported raw materials consumed, $M^*_{it}$.

Enforcement was weak. Tax evasion in Colombia was high during the sample period [@Sanchez1994], and the tax authority had an inefficient auditing system, was overburdened, and faced legal loopholes [@Perry1990].

## Juridical organizations: corporations as non-evaders {#sec-setting-jo}

Corporations were the firms least likely to overreport, for three reasons. First, the Superintendent of Corporations closely monitored them by requiring an auditor. Second, freely tradable shares create an incentive to be profitable: if a corporation falsely reports lower profits, the value of its shares would likely fall, scaring away shareholders and potential investors. Consistent with this, stock prices of public corporations fall, on average, when news of their involvement in tax shelters becomes public [@HanlonSlemrod2009; @Slemrod2019, p. 909, fn. 7]. Third, shareholders pay the individual income tax only on distributed dividends, so a corporation has an additional margin: through its dividend policy, it decides when its owners pay. Partnerships and LLCs have no such margin, since their owners are taxed on all profits.

The data distinguish several juridical organizations; I keep four: corporations, limited liability companies (LLCs), partnerships, and proprietorships (@tbl-jo-summary). Corporations (*sociedades anónimas*) are associations of capital, the counterpart of the US corporation: at least five shareholders, tradable shares of equal value, and liability limited to the capital contributed [@FiscalSurveyColombia1965]. An LLC (*sociedad de responsabilidad limitada*) has two or more partners, not exceeding 20 [@FiscalSurveyColombia1965] or 25 [@DANE2018], whose shares cannot be traded and whose liability is limited to the capital contributed; it is an association of persons, not of capital, and is not subject to the Superintendent of Corporations unless more than one-third of it is owned by a corporation [@FiscalSurveyColombia1965]. Partnerships are associations of two or more persons who are jointly and severally liable for the partnership's operations; they are a small group (3.5% of firm-years), pooled with the other unincorporated firms. Proprietorships are individuals who allocate part of their assets to conduct commercial activities.

![Juridical organization, manufacturing firms in Colombia (1981--1991).](/tables/ch03-jo-summary.png){#tbl-jo-summary}

The other organizations in the data are excluded: stock partnerships (*sociedades en comandita por acciones*), whose shares are tradable and which are taxed as corporations [@FiscalSurveyColombia1965], and non-profit or state organizations, such as cooperatives, community enterprises, and state industrial enterprises, whose proceeds come from taxes, fees, or special contributions.

The juridical organizations faced different income-tax rates. Since the 1974 reform, corporations were taxed at 40% of their income, and partnerships and LLCs at 20% [@McLure1989; @PerryCardenas1986, vol. 1, p. 23]. Proprietors were subject to the graduated individual schedule, with a top rate of 56% [@PerryCardenas1986, vol. 1, p. 36]. Owners were taxed again at the individual level, but differently: shareholders paid tax only on the dividends they received, whereas owners of partnerships and LLCs paid tax on their share of the profits, whether distributed or not [@McLure1989]. The income of proprietorships was taxed only once, at the individual level. Because materials are a deductible cost, overreporting them also lowers the income tax, so the reward to overreporting varied within industries too, with the juridical organization.

## The 1983 reform {#sec-setting-st}

The 1983 reform raised the sales-tax rate for most of manufacturing but left food products exempt. It combined the items previously taxed at 6 and 15 percent into a single 10 percent bracket [@Perry1990, p. 182], while food products (industries 311 and 312), exempt since the tax was introduced [@Perry1990, p. 181], stayed exempt. For most firms this was an increase: between 1983 and 1985, the median rate on sales rose from 6% to 10%, and the median rate on purchases, the rate at which each fictitious peso of materials is credited, from 6.6% to 9.9% (@tbl-st-by-year).

The new rate applied from 1 April 1984 [@CorteConstitucional2016; @Perry1990], so 1983 is the last full pre-reform year and 1984 a partial one. The observed rates match this timing (@tbl-st-by-year). The median rate paid on sales is 6% in 1981–1983, 10% from 1985, and 12% in 1991, after Ley 49 de 1990 raised the general rate to 12% [@Ley49_1990]. In 1984 it is 9%, exactly what three months at 6% and nine months at 10% give ($0.25\times6\%+0.75\times10\%=9\%$).

:::{#tbl-st-by-year}
![](/tables/ch03-st-by-year.png)

Observed sales-tax rates by survey year, on sales ($\tau_S$) and on purchases ($\tau_P$), against the statutory general rate in force. Rows in bold are the years a reform took effect: 1984 (Decreto 3541 de 1983, from 1 April) and 1991 (Ley 49 de 1990, from 1 January). Firms with a rate strictly between 0 and 50%.
:::

The same law, Ley 9 de 1983, also cut income-tax rates. The individual schedule, faced by proprietorships, fell by 4.6 percentage points on average, with the top rate falling from 56% to 49%, and the LLC rate fell from 20% to 18% [@PerryCardenas1986, vol. 1, p. 36].

The reform followed a public debate. The Bird–Wiesner Mission (1978–1981), a technical mission on Colombia's intergovernmental finances led by Richard Bird and Eduardo Wiesner, reported in 1981 [@JunguitoRincon2004]; among its recommendations were better tax administration to reduce evasion, stronger collection tools, wider withholding, and more auditing [@Bolanos2019]. Using the extraordinary powers granted by article 53 of Ley 9 de 1983, the government issued Decreto 3541 on 29 December 1983. It set the general sales-tax rate at 10% (art. 6), extended the tax to the retail level as a value-added tax, and took effect on 1 April 1984 (art. 92) [@Decreto3541_1983; @Perry1990].

::: {.content-visible when-meta="draft"}
**Draft block: the 1986 reform (Hans, 2026-09-26: kept in draft until deciding whether to open that door; all 1986 material lives here, @sec-fiscal only points to it).**

In 1986, Ley 75 cut income-tax rates again. It set the entity-level rate for corporations and LLCs at 30%, down from 40% for corporations and up from 18% for LLCs, and ended the double taxation of owners by exempting dividends and LLC profit shares from the individual income tax [@JunguitoRincon2004; @McLure1989]. The individual schedule was reduced to four marginal rates, with a top rate of 30%. Because LLC owners had been taxed on all profits at the individual level, the combined marginal tax on an LLC's profits fell for most owners despite the higher entity-level rate; it rose only for owners in individual brackets below about 15%. The reform also moved the filing and collection of the income tax to the banking system [@JunguitoRincon2004; @Sanchez1994].
